Lecture 1 — Introduction to Optimization
15.C57 Optimization (Saurabh Amin, Swati Gupta) This first lecture places optimization within data science, defines the vocabulary of an optimization problem, surveys the main classes of problems the course will cover, and introduces linear optimization through three modeling examples. PART 1 — THE SCOPE OF OPTIMIZATION From data to decisions. Analytics has three layers:
- Descriptive analytics (data management, visualization) answers "What happened?"
- Predictive analytics (machine learning, forecasting) answers "What will happen?"
- Prescriptive analytics (optimization, simulation) answers "What should I do?"
Optimization is the prescriptive layer. It handles complex decision-making problems that involve many interdependent decisions and several interrelated constraints. Optimization inside predictive AI (training models). Machine-learning models depend on many parameters — regression coefficients in linear/logistic regression, the tree structure and splits in decision trees and ensembles, the weights in neural networks. These parameters are estimated by minimizing a loss function, which is itself a (usually non-linear) optimization problem. Training a network with weights W on n examples solves
    min_W (1/n) sum_{i=1}^n L(g(x_i, W), y_i),
where g(x_i, W) is the model's prediction. The same non-linear optimization machinery shows up in signal processing, robotics, and elsewhere. Optimization inside prescriptive AI (decision-making). Business, policy, and engineering involve complex decisions — transportation and logistics, workforce management, disaster response, robot path planning. Optimization turns large volumes of data into decisions that improve system performance. Its ingredients: inputs (parameters from data pipelines and predictive models), outputs (the decisions), an objective function (cost, profit, service level, ...), and constraints (requirements and system dynamics). Because the decisions interact, they must be optimized globally. A tale of two problems. Compare two decisions to see where optimization matters most:
- Approving loan applications. The hard part is predicting who will repay. Once you have that prediction, the decision is simple: fund the likely repayers, decline the rest. The difficulty lives in the predictive layer. - Planning electricity generation.

The hard part is predicting who will repay. Once you have that prediction, the decision is simple: fund the likely repayers, decline the rest. The difficulty lives in the predictive layer. - Planning electricity generation. Even with perfect demand predictions, deciding how much each plant should produce is hard, because of spatio-temporal dependencies across the network and over a planning horizon. All the decisions must be jointly optimized. The difficulty lives in the prescriptive (optimization) layer. A little history. Optimization has deep roots:
- Fermat, Newton (1600s): min f(x)  =>  df/dx = 0. - Euler (1755): min f(x_1,...,x_n)  =>  grad f(x) = 0. - Lagrange (1797): min f(x) subject to g_i(x) = 0 for all i  =>  form the Lagrangian L(x) = f(x) + sum_i lambda_i g_i(x). Complexity and tractability. In theory, "efficient" has been equated with "polynomially solvable." But in practice that equation is too pessimistic: "inefficient" does not mean intractable — NP-hard problems are solved routinely at realistic sizes. The course's goal is practically tractable methods that solve realistic-size problems in appropriate computational times, not worst-case guarantees. Why now. Optimization technology has improved staggeringly. Integer-optimization software sped up about 29,000x (CPLEX, 1991–2007) and another 53x (Gurobi, 2009–2019), a cumulative ~1,500,000x, and hardware added roughly another 1,500,000x. Problems that once took hours with dozens of variables are now solved in seconds or minutes with millions of variables and constraints. Optimization is used across transportation, energy, supply chain, health care, finance, and sports — modeling and algorithmic tools at the core of data science. PART 2 — OPTIMIZATION TERMINOLOGY A general optimization problem is written (equivalently) in extended, vector, and compact forms:
    min  f(x_1,...,x_n)          min  f(x)            min  f(x)
    s.t. g_1(x_1,...,x_n) <= 0   s.t. g_1(x) <= 0     s.t. g_i(x) <= 0 for all i
         ... ... g_m(x_1,...,x_n) <= 0        g_m(x) <= 0
The pieces:
- Objective function: f : R^n -> R, measures solution quality. - Constraint functions: g_i : R^n -> R, for i = 1,...,m, encode system requirements. - Feasible region: F = { x in R^n : g_i(x) <= 0 for all i = 1,...,m }. - Decision variable: x in F, the quantities we choose. - Optimal solution: x* in argmin_{x in F} f(x).

- Constraint functions: g_i : R^n -> R, for i = 1,...,m, encode system requirements. - Feasible region: F = { x in R^n : g_i(x) <= 0 for all i = 1,...,m }. - Decision variable: x in F, the quantities we choose. - Optimal solution: x* in argmin_{x in F} f(x). PART 3 — CLASSES OF OPTIMIZATION PROBLEMS Linear optimization (LO). Continuous variables, a linear objective, and linear constraints. Very efficient algorithms scale to millions of variables and constraints. min c^T x  s.t. A x >= b,  x >= 0. Mixed-integer optimization (MIO). Linear optimization with some discrete variables. Mixed-integer: x in Z^p x R^{n-p}. Integer: x in Z^n. Binary: x in {0,1}^n. Modern MIO algorithms scale to thousands or millions of variables. min c^T x  s.t. A x >= b,  x in Z^p_+ x R^{n-p}_+. Optimization under uncertainty. Decisions often must be made without perfect information about current or future conditions. Data uncertainty covers inaccuracy, missing values, and measurement error; core uncertainty means decisions are made before critical information is revealed. Two approaches:
- Stochastic optimization (SO): describe uncertainty by a set S of scenarios, each scenario s with probability p_s, and minimize expected cost:
      min  sum_{s in S} p_s (c_s^T x_s)  s.t. A_s x_s = b_s and x_s >= 0 for all s. - Robust optimization (RO): describe uncertainty by an uncertainty set U and minimize the worst-case cost:
      min c^T x  s.t. A x = b for all A in U,  x >= 0. Non-linear optimization (NLO). A non-linear objective and/or constraints:
    min f(x)  s.t. g_i(x) <= 0 for all i,  x >= 0,   with f, g_i : R^n -> R. Important sub-classes: unconstrained optimization; convex optimization (f and all g_i convex); convex quadratic optimization (g_i(x) = x^T Q_i x + p_i^T x + q_i with Q_i positive semidefinite); non-convex quadratic optimization (Q_i not PSD); and second-order conic optimization. PART 4 — LINEAR OPTIMIZATION: THREE MODELING EXAMPLES The knapsack problem. Packing for a trip: n items j = 1,...,n; item j has unit value c_j and unit volume a_j; total volume capacity b. Decision variable x_j = amount of item j to carry. Maximize value subject to capacity and non-negativity:
    max  sum_j c_j x_j   s.t. sum_j a_j x_j <= b,   x_j >= 0 for all j. The manufacturing (production planning) problem. A facility makes n products from m raw materials. Data: profit pi_j of product j; available units b_i of material i; a_ij units of material i needed per unit of product j. Decision variable x_j = amount of product j manufactured. Maximize total profit subject to material availability:
    max  sum_j pi_j x_j   s.t. sum_j a_ij x_j <= b_i for all i,   x_j >= 0 for all j. Insight: constraints couple products (they compete for shared materials) and couple materials. Many resource constraints turn out non-binding at the optimum. Against a greedy benchmark (sort products by unit profit and produce each in turn until a resource is depleted), the optimal solution here raises profit by 12%. The edge of optimization comes from thinking globally rather than locally — a high-unit-profit product may be worth producing less of so that shared materials are freed for a more profitable overall mix. The transportation problem. A logistics provider ships a product from m plants to n warehouses. Data: plant capacity s_i; warehouse demand d_j; unit shipping cost c_ij from plant i to warehouse j. Decision variable x_ij = units shipped from i to j. Minimize total cost subject to meeting demand and respecting capacity:
    min  sum_i sum_j c_ij x_ij
    s.t.

Data: plant capacity s_i; warehouse demand d_j; unit shipping cost c_ij from plant i to warehouse j. Decision variable x_ij = units shipped from i to j. Minimize total cost subject to meeting demand and respecting capacity:
    min  sum_i sum_j c_ij x_ij
    s.t. sum_i x_ij >= d_j for all j    (meet each warehouse's demand),
         sum_j x_ij <= s_i for all i    (respect each plant's capacity),
         x_ij >= 0 for all i, j. Note the decision variable is a vector in the manufacturing problem but a matrix in the transportation problem — structure your variables as functions of the index sets. PART 5 — STRUCTURE OF LINEAR OPTIMIZATION MODELS General form and standard form. The general form of an LO allows >=, <=, and = constraints and variables that are >= 0, <= 0, or free:
    min/max c^T x  s.t. a_i^T x >= b_i (i in M1),  a_i^T x <= b_i (i in M2),  a_i^T x = b_i (i in M3);  x_j >= 0 (j in N1),  x_j <= 0 (j in N2),  x_j free (j in N3). The standard form is
    min c^T x  s.t. A x = b,  x >= 0. Every LO can be written in standard form. The conversions:
- Maximization to minimization:  max c^T x  =  -min (-c)^T x. - Inequality to equality (slack/surplus variables):  a_i^T x <= b_i  becomes  a_i^T x + s_i = b_i with s_i >= 0;  a_i^T x >= b_i  becomes  a_i^T x - s_i = b_i with s_i >= 0. - Free variable to non-negative parts:  x free  becomes  x = x^+ - x^- with x^+, x^- >= 0. In practice you write a formulation in general form and the solver converts it to standard form internally. The modeling power of linear optimization. LO can capture more than it first appears. Minimizing a sum of absolute values with non-negative weights,
    min sum_j c_j |x_j|  s.t. A x >= b   (with c_j >= 0),
is linearized by introducing z_j and writing
    min sum_j c_j z_j  s.t. A x >= b,  z_j >= x_j,  z_j >= -x_j  for all j. More generally, a piecewise-linear convex cost C(x_j) = max_k ( d_kj^T x_j + g_kj ) is modeled with
    min sum_j z_j  s.t. A x >= b,  z_j >= d_kj^T x_j + g_kj for all j, k. So linear optimization models piecewise-linear convex functions exactly and approximates general convex functions. A workflow for building formulations:
- Structure your data consistently. Define the index sets (categories) first, then define every numerical parameter as a function of those sets.

So linear optimization models piecewise-linear convex functions exactly and approximates general convex functions. A workflow for building formulations:
- Structure your data consistently. Define the index sets (categories) first, then define every numerical parameter as a function of those sets. - Define decision variables clearly and consistently, again as functions of the sets (a vector for manufacturing, a matrix for transportation). - Write the linear objective and linear constraints — physical requirements, managerial requirements, system dynamics — capturing interdependencies that force global optimization. A single objective can encode multi-objective trade-offs and blend hard and soft constraints. As Laszlo Lovasz put it, if you tallied which mathematical problem uses the most computer time in the world, the answer would probably be linear optimization. PART 6 — CONCLUSION Common themes across optimization: data availability (defining sets and input parameters from historical data); problem definition (operations, scheduling, planning); benefits of integration (longer horizons, larger scale and scope, at the cost of larger, more complex models); multi-objective optimization (trading off competing objectives, hard vs. soft constraints); the impact of uncertainty (solutions that perform well across many scenarios, even adverse ones); distributed optimization (many decision-makers with their own objectives); and computational time (real-time optimization in seconds vs. strategic planning in minutes or hours). Takeaways:
- Optimization is used broadly across industries to turn data into decisions. - A model has four components: inputs, decision variables, an objective, and constraints. - Optimization modeling is both a science and an art. - The main classes are linear optimization, mixed-integer optimization, optimization under uncertainty, and non-linear optimization. - Linear optimization is a critical technique for modeling large-scale, important problems that arise in practice.

Recitation 1 — Optimization Basics, Recognizing Linear Optimization, and Standard Form
15.C57 Optimization (Madeleine Pollack) This first recitation builds the vocabulary of an optimization model, practices recognizing when a problem is a linear optimization (LP), converts general LPs to standard form, works two modeling exercises, and closes with a Julia crash course for implementing and solving a model. PART 1 — THE OPTIMIZATION SKELETON What is optimization? Mathematical optimization is the selection of a best element (the optimal solution), with regard to some criteria (the objective), from a set of available alternatives (the feasible region defined by the constraints). Common objectives are maximizing profit or efficiency and minimizing risk; common application areas include healthcare, policy-making, and manufacturing; optimization intersects computer science, statistics, data science, economics, finance, and many engineering disciplines. Terminology. A general optimization problem is
    min_x  f(x)   s.t. g_i(x) <= 0,  i = 1,...,m. The parts of the "skeleton" you should be able to identify in any problem:
- Inputs / parameters: quantities known before solving — costs, capacities, demands, processing times, etc. - Decision variables: the quantities we choose, collected in x in R^n. - Objective function: f : R^n -> R, measuring solution quality. - Constraints: g_i : R^n -> R, encoding system requirements. - Feasible region: F = { x in R^n : g_i(x) <= 0 for all i = 1,...,m }. - Optimal solution: x* in argmin_{x in F} f(x). When you meet a new problem, name each of these six pieces before writing anything down. PART 2 — RECOGNIZING LINEAR OPTIMIZATION A problem is a linear optimization (LP) when the objective and all constraints are linear in the decision variables:
    min/max  c^T x   s.t. a_i^T x <= b_i for all i,   x in R^n,
with a linear objective c^T x and linear equality/inequality constraints. Continuous variables are allowed. A problem is NOT an LP when it contains, for example:
- Integer restrictions: x_1 in Z, or x_1 in {0,1}. - Bilinear terms: x_1 x_2 = 0. - Quadratic terms: x_1^2 + x_2^2 <= 1. - Other non-linear constraints: max{x_1, x_2} >= 5, or ||x||_2 <= 1. Quick check — LP or not? - 3 x_1 - 2 x_2 <= 7 : LP (linear inequality). - x_1 + x_2 = 4 : LP (linear equality). - x_1 in Z_+ : not LP (integrality).

- Bilinear terms: x_1 x_2 = 0. - Quadratic terms: x_1^2 + x_2^2 <= 1. - Other non-linear constraints: max{x_1, x_2} >= 5, or ||x||_2 <= 1. Quick check — LP or not? - 3 x_1 - 2 x_2 <= 7 : LP (linear inequality). - x_1 + x_2 = 4 : LP (linear equality). - x_1 in Z_+ : not LP (integrality). - x_1 x_2 <= 5 : not LP (bilinear product of variables). - x_1^2 + x_2^2 <= 1 : not LP (quadratic). - max{x_1, x_2} <= t : LP-representable — max{x_1, x_2} <= t is equivalent to the two linear constraints x_1 <= t and x_2 <= t. Some non-linear expressions can be linearized:
- Absolute value: |z| <= t is equivalent to the pair z <= t and -z <= t. - Maximum: max{z_1, z_2} <= t is equivalent to z_1 <= t and z_2 <= t. A caution about direction. Suppose you want to force t = |z| and instead write only t >= z and t >= -z:
- If z = 2, those constraints allow any t >= 2 — not only t = 2 — so they do NOT by themselves pin t to |z|. - The trick works when the model pushes t down: if you MINIMIZE t (with only these constraints on t), the optimum drives t to |z|. If you MAXIMIZE t, t runs off and the equality is lost. - The reverse bound does not linearize the same way: |z| >= t is a lower bound on a convex function and CANNOT be captured by requiring z >= t and -z >= t (those two are jointly infeasible unless t <= -|z|). Bounding an absolute value from below is non-convex. The lesson: epigraph-style linearizations of |z| and max{...} are valid for UPPER bounds and when the objective's direction makes them tight; they do not give lower bounds for free. PART 3 — STANDARD FORM General form of a linear optimization allows mixed constraint and variable types:
    min/max c^T x
    s.t. a_i^T x >= b_i  for i in M1,
         a_i^T x <= b_i  for i in M2,
         a_i^T x = b_i   for i in M3,
         x_j >= 0, or x_j <= 0, or x_j free. Standard form is the tidy version every solver reduces to:
    min c^T x   s.t. A x = b,  x >= 0. Converting to standard form:
- Maximization to minimization:  max c^T x  =  -min (-c)^T x. - "<=" constraint: add a slack variable. a^T x <= b  becomes  a^T x + s = b,  s >= 0. - ">=" constraint: subtract a surplus variable. a^T x >= b  becomes  a^T x - s = b,  s >= 0. - Non-positive variable: negate it. x <= 0  becomes  x = -x' with x' >= 0. - Free variable: split into positive and negative parts. x free  becomes  x = x^+ - x^-,  x^+, x^- >= 0. PART 4 — EXERCISES

- ">=" constraint: subtract a surplus variable. a^T x >= b  becomes  a^T x - s = b,  s >= 0. - Non-positive variable: negate it. x <= 0  becomes  x = -x' with x' >= 0. - Free variable: split into positive and negative parts. x free  becomes  x = x^+ - x^-,  x^+, x^- >= 0. PART 4 — EXERCISES Exercise 1: production planning. A manufacturer produces two liquid products, A and B. - Each unit of A earns $5 profit and uses 2 hours of labor and 1 unit of raw material. - Each unit of B earns $4 profit and uses 1 hour of labor and 2 units of raw material. - At most 100 labor hours and 80 units of raw material are available. - A customer contract requires at least 10 units of product B. Tasks: (1) define the inputs and decision variables; (2) formulate an LP that maximizes profit; (3) convert the model to standard form. Setup for discussion: let x_A, x_B be the units produced. The natural formulation is
    max 5 x_A + 4 x_B
    s.t. 2 x_A + 1 x_B <= 100   (labor),
         1 x_A + 2 x_B <= 80    (raw material),
         x_B >= 10              (contract),
         x_A, x_B >= 0. Standard form adds slack/surplus variables (s_1, s_2 for the two "<=" limits, s_3 for the ">=" contract) and negates the objective. Exercise 2: staffing with an imbalance penalty. A consulting team allocates analyst hours between projects A and B. - At least 80 total analyst hours must be assigned, and at most 100 hours are available. - Project A requires at least 25 hours; project B requires at least 20 hours. - Each hour on A costs $120; each hour on B costs $100. - Management adds a penalty of $30 per hour of imbalance between the two projects. Let x_A, x_B be the hours assigned. Tasks: (1) write the natural formulation using |x_A - x_B|; (2) reformulate as an LP; (3) convert to standard form. Setup for discussion: the natural objective is
    min 120 x_A + 100 x_B + 30 |x_A - x_B|. Because we are minimizing, the absolute value linearizes: introduce t with t >= x_A - x_B and t >= x_B - x_A, replace the penalty term with 30 t, and add the hour constraints (x_A + x_B >= 80, x_A + x_B <= 100, x_A >= 25, x_B >= 20, x_A, x_B >= 0). Standard form then follows by the slack/surplus and objective-sign rules above. This is exactly the linearization from Part 2, made legitimate by the minimization direction.
